newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Rightist lunatic fringe blamed in S.African blasts.
newsitem.headline: Rightist lunatic fringe blamed in S.African blasts.

text.p: South Africa has little to fear from those responsible for bomb attacks at the weekend and on Christmas Eve, political analysts said, attributing the blasts to a right-wing lunatic fringe.

The ruling African National Congress called the bombs "an attempt to stir hostile emotions with a view to undermining the stability of our democracy", but analysts did not see them as heralding any major resurgence of white resistance to black rule.
"I think it's a small bunch of desperadoes who are not going to last very long...There's no kind of wave of right-wing action," said David Welsh, professor of politics at the University of Cape Town.

Four people were killed in the first bombing in Worcester, near Cape Town, on December 24 and two people were hurt at the weekend by a bomb which was detonated at a mosque in Rustenburg, northwest of Johannesburg.

Police are hunting three right-wing whites in connection with the Worcester attack, naming them as fugitive murderers already convicted in absentia for a series of bombs which exploded on the eve of South Africa's first all-race elections in April 1994.

Statements issued on behalf of a previously unknown group called Boere Attack Troops (BAT) claimed responsibility for both bombings. The group demanded, among other things, the removal of all Indians from the government and described Moslems as "the anti-Christ".
"They have much in common with similar nutty groups in the United States which have these weird religious beliefs," Welsh said. "You can only call them bizarre."

Jakkie Cilliers, director of the independent Institute for Defence Policy think tank, said whoever carried out the bombings could have been reacting to the emergence of a Cape Town-based Moslem vigilante group called People Against Gangsterism and Drugs (Pagad).

"The old National Party state was based on a Christian, Calvinist ethic, and now we have the very clear surgence of a Moslem fundamentalist movement...which is seen as having been allowed to take the law into their own hands," he said.
Cilliers said this had a "demonstrative" effect for right-wing whites, who felt alienated from the state since the ANC victory in the 1994 election.

"To a degree people overestimate the degree of reconciliation there has been," he said. "But nationwide the sting has been removed from the right wing. They pose more of a criminal threat than a political threat."
Right-wing whites demanding self-rule in an independent Afrikaner state frequently threatened civil war in the run-up to the 1994 poll.

But the potential for concerted armed resistance was largely eliminated when a key right-wing leader, former defence force chief General Constand Viljoen, decided to contest the elections and take his party into parliament.
Many of the right-wing groups that proliferated in South Africa ahead of the elections were, in the words of one political analyst, "one man, his dog and a fax machine".

The bombings were condemned on Monday by a mainstream right- wing politician, Conservative Party leader Ferdi Hartzenberg, who said they played into the hands of President Nelson Mandela's government.
"The attacks distract attention from the government's sorry record...Actions like these damage the just cause of the Afrikaner," he said in a statement.
